points: 〜てあげる／てくれる／てもらう

title: Favors
titleJp: 友だちがてつだってくれました
canDo: I can tell about a favor I did for someone with 〜てあげる, using the particle the verb asks for: 友だちにかさを貸してあげました。
I can tell about a favor someone did for me or my family with 〜てくれる: 田中さんが駅まで送ってくれました。
I can say I received (or asked for) a favor with [person]に 〜てもらう, and tell the same scene with 〜てくれる.
I can explain who gets the benefit in each form, linking it to あげる / くれる / もらう from lesson 14-2.
I can offer help to a superior with 〜ましょうか, without the 〜てあげます that sounds arrogant.

blocks.t: Warm-up: say the て-form of 貸す, 持つ, 起こす, 送る, 教える, 読む and なおす out loud, then one sentence each with あげる, くれる and もらう (lesson 14-2)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar: the 3 points, each with its examples read aloud and one 🔬. In your notebook, draw an arrow for each form: which way does the favor go?
Block 6: the Lesson 16 video (only the part about favors) or the Sakubi sections, as a second explanation
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: あげる, くれる and もらう with things (lesson 14-2): who gives, who receives, and the job of に. This lesson uses exactly the same directions, now with actions.
The て-form of every verb, without hesitating (lesson 06-1): 貸して, 持って, 読んで, 起こして, 送って. All three favors are て-form + a verb of giving or receiving.
〜ましょうか to offer help (lesson 06-4). It replaces 〜てあげる when you talk to a superior.

vocab.en: to wake someone up ([person]を起こす)
to take, walk or drive someone somewhere ([person]を送る); to send
to teach; to tell, to show (道を教える = to tell someone the way)
to fix, to repair; to correct

grammar.title: 〜てあげる
grammar.gloss: doing something for someone (the favor goes outward)
grammar.explanation:
In lesson 14-2 you saw あげる, くれる and もらう with **things**. Now what passes from one person to another is an **action**: a favor. The recipe is always the same: **て-form of the verb + あげる / くれる / もらう**. It is the X て Y pattern again (〜てみる, 〜ておく): the giving verb no longer hands over a thing; it says **who the action is for**. The directions are also the same as in lesson 14-2, and the key question is: **who gets the benefit?**
• 〜てあげる: **I (or someone) do something for another person**. The benefit leaves the doer and goes **outward**, as with あげる. The one doing the favor is the TOPIC: 私は, ルーカスさんは.
• The iron rule: in an ordinary statement, the one who receives a 〜てあげる favor is **never you**, nor anyone on your side. A favor that comes to you needs くれる (point b). That rule is what lets Japanese drop the people: 貸してあげた, with no names at all, usually means "I lent it to someone".
• The person who receives the favor takes **the particle the verb would take without あげる**. 貸す and 教える take に (友だちに貸す) → 友だちに貸してあげる. 起こす and てつだう take を (妹を起こす) → 妹を起こしてあげる. If the favor is about something that belongs to the person, use の: おばあさんのかばんを持ってあげる.
• English marks the favor with "for (someone)". Japanese marks it in the verb, with あげる, so there is no separate word for "for".
• With verbs that have no slot for a person, like 作る and 買う, you can leave the person out (the context shows who it is) or use [person]のために, "for [person]": 友だちのためにケーキを作ってあげました.
• 貸してあげました is **a single block: the PREDICATE**. Read from it: "lent, as a favor" → what? → to whom?

**Careful with superiors.** 〜てあげる casts you as the one doing a favor. Said directly to a superior (a teacher, a boss, a customer), 先生、にもつを持ってあげます sounds like "I'll do you the favor of carrying it" and can come across as arrogant. To offer help, use **〜ましょうか** (lesson 06-4): 先生、にもつを持ちましょうか。 Telling someone about a favor that another person did (ルーカスさんはおばあさんのかばんを持ってあげました) is fine.
• Going further (Sakubi): games and anime use a rougher cousin, **〜てやる**. Toward a pet or a much younger family member it just means "do for" (犬とあそんでやる); in a quarrel, it means doing something at someone's expense: おまえのプリンも食べてやる！ ("I'll eat your pudding too — so there!"). Understand it, but say 〜てあげる yourself.
grammar.structure: [doer] は [receiver + the verb's particle] [object] を [て-form] あげる

examples.jp: ルーカスさんはおばあさんのかばんを持ってあげました。
examples.kana: ルーカスさんはおばあさんのかばんをもってあげました。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu-san wa obāsan no kaban o motte agemashita.
examples.en: Lucas carried the elderly lady's bag for her.

examples.jp: 私はマリアさんに日本の地図を貸してあげました。
examples.kana: わたしはマリアさんににほんのちずをかしてあげました。
examples.romaji: Watashi wa Maria-san ni Nihon no chizu o kashite agemashita.
examples.en: I lent Maria a map of Japan (as a favor to her).

examples.jp: 朝七時に妹を起こしてあげました。
examples.kana: あさしちじにいもうとをおこしてあげました。
examples.romaji: Asa shichiji ni imōto o okoshite agemashita.
examples.en: I woke my little sister up at seven in the morning (as a favor to her).

pitfalls: Don't use 〜てあげる directly with a superior: 先生、にもつを持ってあげます ✗ (sounds arrogant) → 先生、にもつを持ちましょうか ✓.
The person takes the verb's own particle, not always に: 妹に起こしてあげました ✗ → 妹を起こしてあげました ✓ (起こす takes を).
The favor of あげる goes outward, never to you: 友だちが私にかさを貸してあげました ✗ → 友だちがかさを貸してくれました ✓ (point b).
howToStudy: Say out loud 3 favors you did in the last few days, each with the right particle: 〜に貸してあげました, 〜を起こしてあげました, 〜の〜を持ってあげました.

Tap 🔬 on example 1: ルーカスさんは is the TOPIC (who does the favor), おばあさんの is DESCRIBES NEXT (whose bag), かばんを is the OBJECT and 持ってあげました is the PREDICATE. Start reading from the predicate: "carried, as a favor" → what? → whose?
Take 3 sentences with 〜てあげます and turn them into offers with 〜ましょうか, as if you were talking to a teacher: 持ってあげます → 持ちましょうか。
grammar.flag: Check in your Genki II that this lesson has these points in this order.

grammar.title: 〜てくれる
grammar.gloss: someone does something for me (the favor comes my way)
grammar.explanation:
〜てくれる: **someone does something for me**, or for someone on my side (family, friends, my group). The benefit comes **toward the speaker**, just like くれる in lesson 14-2.
• The one doing the favor is the SUBJECT and usually takes **が**: 田中さんが送ってくれました.
• The receiver almost never appears: くれる already says it was me. You don't need 私に or 私を in every sentence.
• So the last verb tells you who is who, even when nobody is named: 起こしてくれた = someone woke **me** (or someone on my side) up; 起こしてあげた = usually **I** woke someone up. When you read, let the verb at the end show you which way the arrow goes.
• It also works for your group: ペドロさんが弟に日本語を教えてくれました (my brother is on my side).
• The particles are still the verb's own: 教える takes に (弟に), and 送る takes を for the person being taken somewhere (私を, which disappears).
• Japanese tends to **mark the favor** when someone does something good for you. 母が作りました just reports the fact; 母が作ってくれました shows that you appreciate the kindness. English often does this with "for me" or with your tone of voice; Japanese does it in the verb.
• In a question, くれる points toward the listener: だれがてつだってくれましたか = "who helped you?".
• Preview: to thank someone for a favor, Japanese uses 〜てくれて、ありがとう ("thanks for…"). It comes back properly in lesson 19-2.
grammar.structure: [doer] が ([私に / 私を]) [object] を [て-form] くれる

examples.jp: 田中さんが駅まで車で送ってくれました。
examples.kana: たなかさんがえきまでくるまでおくってくれました。
examples.romaji: Tanaka-san ga eki made kuruma de okutte kuremashita.
examples.en: Mr./Ms. Tanaka drove me to the station.

examples.jp: ペドロさんが弟に日本語を教えてくれました。
examples.kana: ペドロさんがおとうとににほんごをおしえてくれました。
examples.romaji: Pedoro-san ga otōto ni nihongo o oshiete kuremashita.
examples.en: Pedro taught my little brother Japanese (a favor to my family).

examples.jp: だれがてつだってくれましたか。— アナさんがてつだってくれました。
examples.kana: だれがてつだってくれましたか。— アナさんがてつだってくれました。
examples.romaji: Dare ga tetsudatte kuremashita ka. — Ana-san ga tetsudatte kuremashita.
examples.en: Who helped you? — Ana helped me.

pitfalls: くれる never goes outside your side: 友だちがマリアさんに教えてくれました ✗ (if Maria is not in your group) → 友だちがマリアさんに教えてあげました ✓.
The doer takes が (or は), not に: 田中さんに送ってくれました ✗ → 田中さんが送ってくれました ✓. The に for the doer belongs to 〜てもらう (point c).
You are not the subject of くれる: 私は友だちにてつだってくれました ✗ → 友だちがてつだってくれました ✓, or 私は友だちにてつだってもらいました ✓.
howToStudy: Think of 3 favors you received (from family, friends, colleagues) and say each one out loud with 〜が〜てくれました.
Tap 🔬 on example 2: ペドロさんが is the SUBJECT (the doer), 弟に is the TARGET (who receives it), 日本語を is the OBJECT and 教えてくれました is the PREDICATE. Ask yourself: which way does the favor go? Toward my side.
Read examples 1 and 2 aloud twice, first with くれました and then without it (送りました, 教えました), and notice how the version without くれる sounds like a plain report.

grammar.title: 〜てもらう
grammar.gloss: receiving a favor from someone ([person]に 〜てもらう)
grammar.explanation:
〜てもらう: **I receive a favor from someone**. It is the same scene as 〜てくれる, seen from the other side. The SUBJECT is now **the receiver** (almost always me, so it disappears), and the doer takes **に**.
• 父が自転車をなおしてくれました。 → the doer (父) is the subject, with が.
• 父に自転車をなおしてもらいました。 → the receiver (me) is the hidden subject; the doer comes with に.
• This に is the **source** of the favor, as in 友だちにもらいました (lesson 14-2): "received FROM". It is not the destination.
• English has a close pattern: "I had my dad fix my bike" or "I got my dad to fix my bike" also make the receiver the subject. 〜てもらう works the same way, but it also carries a sense of thanks. It is almost a passive (lesson 21-1): the one who receives the action becomes the subject, and the doer gets に, like "by" in "my bike was fixed by my dad".
• The mirror of the rule in point a: with もらう, the doer in the に block is **never you**. When you did the favor, tell it with あげる: 私はアナさんをてつだってあげました, never アナさんは私にてつだってもらいました.
• 〜てもらう often suggests that **you asked** for the favor, while 〜てくれる highlights the kindness of the doer. In everyday speech both often describe the same event, and you will hear both a lot.
• Read from the predicate: なおしてもらいました = "received the favor of fixing" → from whom? → the block with に.
• With teachers and superiors, the humble version is 〜ていただく (いただく = humble もらう): 先生に説明していただきました. It is the base of the polite request in lesson 16-2.
• Going further (Sakubi): with two other people, the verb also shows whose side you are telling the story from. ルーカスさんがおばあさんに道を教えてあげました is told from Lucas's side; おばあさんはルーカスさんに道を教えてもらいました is told from the lady's side. Same event, different camera.
grammar.structure: [receiver (me)] は [doer] に [object] を [て-form] もらう

examples.jp: 私はすずきさんに写真をとってもらいました。
examples.kana: わたしはすずきさんにしゃしんをとってもらいました。
examples.romaji: Watashi wa Suzuki-san ni shashin o totte moraimashita.
examples.en: Mr./Ms. Suzuki took a photo for me. [lit. as for me, from Suzuki, received the favor of taking a photo]

examples.jp: 日本人の友だちにメールをチェックしてもらいました。
examples.kana: にほんじんのともだちにメールをチェックしてもらいました。
examples.romaji: Nihonjin no tomodachi ni mēru o chekku shite moraimashita.
examples.en: I had a Japanese friend check my e-mail.

examples.jp: 父に自転車をなおしてもらいました。
examples.kana: ちちにじてんしゃをなおしてもらいました。
examples.romaji: Chichi ni jitensha o naoshite moraimashita.
examples.en: My father fixed my bicycle for me (I received that favor from him).

pitfalls: The doer takes に, not が: 友だちがてつだってもらいました ✗ (it would say your friend was the one who got help) → 友だちにてつだってもらいました ✓.
Don't mix up the two に: with あげる, に is the receiver (友だちに貸してあげる); with もらう, に is the doer (友だちに貸してもらう). Always look at the verb at the end.

Favors are for good things only. (someone read your diary without asking) 友だちににっきを読んでもらいました ✗ (it sounds as if you had asked them to) → 友だちがにっきを読みました ✓ for now. The form that shows you suffered from it is the passive (lesson 21-1).
When you are the one who did the favor, もらう can't carry it: アナさんは私にてつだってもらいました ✗ → 私はアナさんをてつだってあげました ✓ (plain てつだいました is fine too, and sounds more modest).
howToStudy: Take the 3 favors you said in point b and tell each one again with 〜てもらう: 〜が〜てくれました → 〜に〜てもらいました.

Drills → 🔬 Anatomy → 🔬 Analyze: paste example 3. The 🔬 tags 父に as TARGET, its general label for a block with に. With もらう, read that に as FROM: 父 is the one who did the favor, not the one who received it.
Record yourself telling 2 favors you asked someone for (a friend, a colleague), with [person]に〜てもらいました.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Use kanji only for the ones you already know and write the rest in kana. Before each item, draw a small arrow: who does the favor → who receives it. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day. If you have the Genki II Workbook, do this lesson's exercises too; in this lesson, the ones on 〜てあげる／てくれる／てもらう.

tasks.prompt: Fill in あげました, くれました or もらいました, following the English.

items.q: 私は弟に日本語を教えて＿。 (I taught my little brother Japanese.)
items.note: The favor leaves me and goes to my brother.

items.q: 友だちが私のレポートを読んで＿。 (My friend read my report for me.)
items.note: The doer (が) is the friend, and the favor comes to me.

items.q: 私は母に駅まで送って＿。 (My mother took me to the station.)
items.note: 母に = the doer; I (私は) received the favor. 送る takes を for the person being taken, so this に can only be the source of the favor.

items.q: アナさんがかさを貸して＿。 (Ana lent me an umbrella.)
items.note: Subject with が + a favor coming to me.

items.q: 私はルーカスさんにてつだって＿。 (Lucas helped me; I asked him to.)
items.note: てつだう takes を for the person being helped. Here に is the doer of the favor, so the verb is もらう.

items.q: 私はおばあさんに道を教えて＿。 (I showed an elderly lady the way.)
items.note: 教える takes に for the person who learns, and I was the one who told: あげる.

tasks.prompt: Tell the same favor from the other point of view: change 〜てくれました into 〜てもらいました.

items.q: 先生が作文を読んでくれました。

a.jp: 先生に作文を読んでもらいました。
a.kana: せんせいにさくぶんをよんでもらいました。
a.romaji: Sensei ni sakubun o yonde moraimashita.

items.note: The doer moves from が to に, and the subject becomes me (hidden).

items.q: 父がパソコンをなおしてくれました。

a.jp: 父にパソコンをなおしてもらいました。
a.kana: ちちにパソコンをなおしてもらいました。
a.romaji: Chichi ni pasokon o naoshite moraimashita.

items.q: マリアさんがブラジル料理を作ってくれました。

a.jp: マリアさんにブラジル料理を作ってもらいました。
a.kana: マリアさんにブラジルりょうりをつくってもらいました。
a.romaji: Maria-san ni burajiru ryōri o tsukutte moraimashita.

items.q: 田中さんが写真をとってくれました。

a.jp: 田中さんに写真をとってもらいました。
a.kana: たなかさんにしゃしんをとってもらいました。
a.romaji: Tanaka-san ni shashin o totte moraimashita.

items.note: The object (写真を) and the action don't change; only the doer's particle and the final verb do.

tasks.prompt: Translate into Japanese. First decide: does the favor go outward (あげる), come to me (くれる), or do I receive it from someone (もらう)?

a.jp: 私はペドロさんにじしょを貸してあげました。
a.kana: わたしはペドロさんにじしょをかしてあげました。
a.romaji: Watashi wa Pedoro-san ni jisho o kashite agemashita.

items.note: 貸す takes に for the receiver.

a.jp: 友だちが起こしてくれました。
a.kana: ともだちがおこしてくれました。

items.note: 私を doesn't need to appear: くれる already says it was me.

items.q: My teacher explained the grammar to me (I asked).

a.jp: 先生にぶんぽうを説明してもらいました。
a.kana: せんせいにぶんぽうをせつめいしてもらいました。
a.romaji: Sensei ni bunpō o setsumei shite moraimashita.

items.note: "I asked" matches もらう. With a teacher, 説明していただきました is even more polite.

a.jp: だれがそのゲームを教えてくれましたか。
a.kana: だれがそのゲームをおしえてくれましたか。
a.romaji: Dare ga sono gēmu o oshiete kuremashita ka.

items.note: In a question, くれる points toward the listener.

items.q: Professor, shall I carry your bag?

a.jp: 先生、かばんを持ちましょうか。
a.kana: せんせい、かばんをもちましょうか。

items.note: With a superior, offer with 〜ましょうか. 持ってあげます would sound arrogant.

items.q: (Tell it from your side) I helped Ana with her homework.

a.jp: 私はアナさんのしゅくだいをてつだってあげました。
a.kana: わたしはアナさんのしゅくだいをてつだってあげました。
a.romaji: Watashi wa Ana-san no shukudai o tetsudatte agemashita.

items.note: You did the favor, so the verb is あげる. アナさんは私にてつだってもらいました ✗: with もらう, the doer can't be you. Plain てつだいました is also correct and sounds more modest.

tasks.prompt: Write 4 true sentences about favors: one with 〜てあげました, one with 〜てくれました, one with 〜てもらいました and one offer of help to a superior with 〜ましょうか. Then read them aloud and record yourself on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: きのう、妹にしゅくだいを教えてあげました。友だちが駅まで送ってくれました。母にケーキを作ってもらいました。先生、にもつを持ちましょうか。
a.kana: きのう、いもうとにしゅくだいをおしえてあげました。ともだちがえきまでおくってくれました。ははにケーキをつくってもらいました。せんせい、にもつをもちましょうか。
a.romaji: Kinō, imōto ni shukudai o oshiete agemashita. Tomodachi ga eki made okutte kuremashita. Haha ni kēki o tsukutte moraimashita. Sensei, nimotsu o mochimashō ka.
a.en: Yesterday I helped my little sister with her homework (I explained it to her). A friend took me to the station. My mother made a cake for me. Professor, shall I carry your things?

items.note: Check: the doer takes は/が with あげる and くれる, and に with もらう; the person's particle follows the verb (に with 教える and 貸す, を with 起こす and てつだう); and no 〜てあげます said to a superior.

practice.what: If you can, play in an N4 area of the game. Whenever a dialogue has 〜てくれる, 〜てもらう or 〜てあげる, pause and say out loud: who did the favor? who received it? Copy 2 of those lines into your notebook and draw the favor's arrow. Save one of them with ⛏ Mining (fill in its new word with the 📖 Dictionary button), so it comes back in your reviews.

Reviews first (🌊 All). Add the block 3 words that are missing from your deck with ⛏ Mining, as whole words (貸す, 起こす, 送る, 自転車…). Kanji tip: 貸 (lend) has 貝 at the bottom, an old symbol for money — the lender is the one with the money, which keeps it apart from 借りる (to borrow). Then Drills → Conjugation: the て-form of 10 verbs, the base of all three favors.

Resources tab → Tadoku's free graded readers (a level 2 or 3 story) or an easy manga you own: stories are full of favors. Each time you meet 〜てくれた, 〜てもらった or 〜てあげた, draw its arrow in your notebook (who → whom). Don't look up every word: follow the story.

Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times. Favors make the predicate long (て・つ・だ・っ・て・く・れ・ま・し・た, 10 beats, with the small っ as a full beat of silence): keep the same even rhythm all the way to the end.
Record the 4 favors from homework h4 in 1 minute or less. Listen and check that each arrow went in the right direction.

culture.title: Lost and found: lost things usually come back
culture.titleJp: おとしもの・わすれもの
culture.body: In Japan, people who find a lost wallet, phone or umbrella usually take it to the **こうばん**, the neighborhood police box, or to the station counter. That is why lost things often make their way back to their owners, many times with the money still inside. In big cities the police receive a huge number of items every year, and umbrellas are among the most common. The law lets the finder ask the owner for a reward, usually 5% to 20% of the value, but many people waive it. If you leave something on a train, ask at the station counter: rail companies usually keep items for a while before sending them to the police.
culture.try: Practice the こうばん scene out loud: すみません、さいふをおとしました。 And when someone returns it: 見つけてくれて、ありがとうございます。 Notice the てくれて: it is the favor that came to you.

checklist: I can explain without looking who gets the benefit in 〜てあげる, 〜てくれる and 〜てもらう, and link each one to あげる / くれる / もらう from lesson 14-2.
I can tell about a favor I did with 〜てあげました, with the particle the verb asks for (に with 貸す, を with 起こす, の with the person's thing).
I can tell about a favor I received with [doer]が〜てくれました, without needing to say 私に.
I can switch the same scene from 〜てくれました to 〜てもらいました, moving the doer from が to に.
I offer help to a superior with 〜ましょうか, not with 〜てあげます.
I never use 〜てあげる for a favor that came to me, nor 〜てもらう for a favor I did: the verb at the end tells me who is who.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
If I have the Genki II Workbook, I did the exercises on 〜てあげる／てくれる／てもらう.
